course.title: Rust Foundations
course.description: Read, run and write small Rust programs with the real compiler checking your work, from printing and variables to ownership, enums, traits and iterators.
course.audience: Someone new to Rust. Some programming in another language helps but isn't needed.

paragraphs: Rust is a programming language built on one demand: the compiler must be able to tell, before a program runs, which part of the program is responsible for every value in it. In C, a program can release a piece of memory and keep using it, and the mistake shows up, if it shows up at all, as a crash or a wrong answer long after the line that caused it. Languages such as Java and Go prevent it with a garbage collector that runs alongside the program, which costs some speed and takes memory management out of the programmer's hands. Rust prevents it while the program is being compiled, by giving every value one owner and checking each use of the value against that fact, and the same checking rules out two parts of a program changing the same data at once.

A compiler that checks this much refuses programs that other languages would accept, and a beginner meets those refusals early and often. Each one is an error message that names the rule that was broken, and most of them show the repair: E0382, for example, reports that a value was used after it had been moved to another owner, and points to both of the lines involved. Reading such messages is therefore the quickest way to learn the rules, and it changes what it means for a program to compile, since a Rust program that builds has already been checked for a whole class of mistakes that other languages leave to testing.

Because nothing runs alongside the program to clean up after it, Rust programs can be about as fast as the equivalent C, and because the checking happens beforehand they can be trusted with work in which a memory error is a security flaw, which is why parts of Firefox and of the Linux kernel are now written in it. The programs here are short enough to be read in full, so every rule can be judged in the same way, by what the compiler says about the program in front of you.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a short Rust program and predict exactly what it prints.
You'll be able to write functions, loops and decisions that compile and produce the output you meant.
You'll be able to explain why a value was moved or a borrow was refused, name the error code (E0382, E0502, E0499, E0597), and fix it.
You'll be able to model data with structs and enums, and handle missing values and failures with Option, Result and ?.
You'll be able to store data in Vec, String and HashMap, and write generic functions, traits and closures.
You'll be able to combine these pieces into a program of about fifty lines that parses data, skips bad input and prints a report.
introduction.prerequisites: Some programming in another language helps, but nothing beyond everyday arithmetic is assumed.

modules.title: First programs
modules.description: Printing, variables, number types and functions.

modules.title: Control flow and ownership
modules.description: Decisions and loops, then the rules that decide who owns a value: moves, borrows and slices.

modules.title: Modelling data
modules.description: Structs and enums, Option and Result for what can be missing or fail, and the standard collections.

modules.title: Abstraction and a whole program
modules.description: Traits, generics, lifetimes, closures and iterators, ending with one program that uses everything.

concepts.title: Variables and printing
concepts.summary: let names a value and println! prints it. Add mut when the value has to change.

concepts.title: Types and functions
concepts.summary: Whole and decimal number types, and functions that return their last expression.

concepts.title: if is an expression
concepts.summary: An if / else evaluates to the value of the branch that runs, so it can sit on the right of let or be the last line of a function, provided every branch has the same type.

concepts.title: Conditions are bool
concepts.summary: The condition of an if must have type bool; Rust never treats numbers or strings as true or false.

concepts.title: loop, while and for
concepts.summary: loop repeats until break and may break with a value, while repeats as long as a bool condition holds, and for visits each item of an iterator such as a range.

concepts.title: Ranges
concepts.summary: a..b runs from a up to but not including b, a..=b includes b, and methods such as rev() and step_by(n) change the order and spacing.

concepts.title: Ownership
concepts.summary: Every value has exactly one owner; when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped, and assigning or passing a non-Copy value to a function moves ownership.

concepts.title: Copy and move
concepts.summary: Simple fixed-size types such as integers, bool and char are copied on assignment; a String or Vec is moved, so the old name cannot be used afterwards.

concepts.title: References
concepts.summary: &x borrows x without taking ownership, &mut x borrows it for changing, and * follows a reference to the value.

concepts.title: The borrow rules
concepts.summary: At any moment a value may have any number of shared references or exactly one mutable reference, never both, and a reference may not outlive the value.

concepts.title: Slices
concepts.summary: A slice such as &[i32] or &str is a borrowed view of part of a sequence, written &x[a..b], and it keeps the whole sequence borrowed while it is in use.

concepts.title: String and &str
concepts.summary: String owns growable UTF-8 text, &str borrows text that someone else owns (a literal or a String), and len() counts bytes, not characters.

concepts.title: Structs
concepts.summary: A struct groups named fields into one type, and a value of it is built with Name { field: value }.

concepts.title: Methods
concepts.summary: Functions in an impl block whose first parameter is self, &self or &mut self are called with dot syntax, while functions without self, such as new, are called with Name::.

concepts.title: Enums
concepts.summary: An enum is a type whose value is exactly one of its named variants, and each variant may carry its own data.

concepts.title: match
concepts.summary: match compares a value against patterns in order, binds the data inside a variant, must cover every case, and is an expression whose arms share one type.

concepts.title: Option
concepts.summary: Option<T> is the standard enum with two variants, Some(value) and None, used wherever a value may be absent, and it is a different type from T so the absence cannot be forgotten.

concepts.title: Unpacking an Option
concepts.summary: match and if let run code for Some(x) and optionally for None, unwrap_or gives a default, and unwrap stops the program if the value is None.

concepts.title: Result
concepts.summary: Result<T, E> is an enum with Ok(value) for success and Err(error) for failure, so a function that can fail says so in its return type and the caller must deal with both.

concepts.title: The ? operator
concepts.summary: Placing ? after a Result gives the Ok value or returns the Err from the current function immediately, and it works only in a function whose return type can carry that error.

concepts.title: Vec
concepts.summary: Vec<T> is a growable list of values of one type, built with vec![] or Vec::new(), extended with push, read with v[i] (which panics out of range) or v.get(i) (which returns an Option).

concepts.title: HashMap
concepts.summary: HashMap<K, V> stores values under keys, insert replaces, get returns an Option, entry(key).or_insert(default) inserts only when the key is absent, and the iteration order is not specified.

concepts.title: Traits
concepts.summary: A trait names behaviour as a set of method signatures, with optional default bodies, and a type opts in with impl Trait for Type.

concepts.title: Generics and trait bounds
concepts.summary: A generic function or struct is written once for any type T, and a bound such as T: PartialOrd + Copy states which operations the body may use on T.

concepts.title: Lifetimes
concepts.summary: A lifetime is the span of code in which a reference is valid, and the compiler checks that no reference is used after the value it points to is gone.

concepts.title: Lifetime annotations
concepts.summary: A signature such as fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str relates the output reference to the inputs so the caller's code can be checked; it does not extend how long anything lives.

concepts.title: Closures
concepts.summary: A closure |x| expression is a small unnamed function that can use variables from the place where it is written, and move captures them by ownership.

concepts.title: Iterator adaptors and consumers
concepts.summary: Adaptors such as map and filter describe a transformation lazily, and nothing runs until a consumer such as sum, count or collect asks for the items.

concepts.title: Composing a program
concepts.summary: A small program is a handful of types and functions where Result carries bad input to one place that decides what to do, collections hold the data, and the borrow rules shape who owns what.

concepts.title: Modules
concepts.summary: mod name { ... } groups items, and pub makes one visible outside its module, so code outside calls it as name::item.

lessons.title: Print a value, then change it

lead.text: Every Rust program that you run begins at a function called **fn main**, whose body is the pair of braces that follows it. The lines inside are carried out in order from the top, and when the last one has finished the program ends, which is why the programs in this lesson share the same outer shape and differ only in what is written between the braces.

The line that produces output is **println!**, which prints its text and then starts a new line. The exclamation mark shows that `println!` is a *macro* and not an ordinary function, a difference that does not matter yet, and the text it prints is written between double quotation marks. Wherever the text contains a pair of braces, Rust fills the gap with one of the values listed after the text, taking the values in order, so that the first `{}` receives the first value, the second `{}` the second, and so on.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the three pairs of braces are filled by 6, 7 and `6 * 7`. The last of these was never written out as a number, because Rust works out `6 * 7` before printing, so **any calculation placed after the text is carried out first and its result is printed**. Both the order of the values and this use of a calculation are needed in the next two exercises.

reveal.text: Matching braces to values by position works for two values and becomes tedious for six, which is one reason the next idea is to give each value a name.

lead.text: Writing `3 + 4` after the text is enough for a single sum, but a program soon needs the same value in several places, and repeating a number would mean changing every copy whenever the number changed. Rust avoids this by letting you attach a name to a value with **let**: the line `let price = 4;` creates the name `price`, gives it the value 4, and from that line onwards `price` can be written wherever 4 could.

A name can be defined from other names, because the right-hand side of a `let` is a calculation like any other. In the figure, `cost` is given the value `price * quantity`, which Rust works out when it reaches that line, and the final `println!` then prints all three names. Inside the braces of the text a name may be written directly, as in `{cost}`, and Rust fills the gap with the value that the name stands for.

afterFigure.text: Each line can use only names that were created *above* it, because the program is carried out from the top and a name that has not yet been created has no value to offer. That is why `cost`, which depends on `price` and `quantity`, comes after both of them. A name made in this way is called a **variable**, although, as the next screens show, in Rust it does not vary unless you ask it to.

reveal.text: Edit the program and run it to check. Changing the 4 in the second line changes the answer without touching any other line, which is the advantage of keeping a value under one name.

The message points at line 3 for the new assignment and at line 2 for the `let` that created `score`, because the fault lies in how the name was made. A name created with a plain `let` is **immutable**: it receives one value and keeps it, so that anyone reading `let score = 10;` can rely on `score` being 10 everywhere below that line.

For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0384`.

lead.text: The repair that rustc suggested is a single word. Writing the word **mut**, short for *mutable*, after `let` tells Rust at the moment a name is created that it will be given new values later, and with that permission an assignment such as `lives = lives - 1` is accepted. The right-hand side is worked out first from the old value and the result then replaces it, so that after the assignment `lives` holds 2 and the 3 is gone.

Rust asks for the permission at the start, and not for the change at the moment it happens, for a reason that grows with the size of a program. When every name is unchangeable unless it is marked, a reader can see at once which names are able to change, and the ones without mut can be set aside when hunting for a value that has gone wrong. The cost to the writer is one word.

afterFigure.text: Only the creation of the variable is marked, and only once: the later assignments are plain lines such as `lives = lives - 1`, with no `let` and no `mut`. Writing `let` again would do something else, which is the subject of the last idea in this lesson.

reveal.text: The edit was made on line 2, where the name is created, and not on line 3, where the change happens: the permission belongs to the let.

lead.text: A different value can also arrive under the same name without `mut`. If a program writes `let amount = 4;` and later `let amount = amount * 3;`, the second line is not an assignment to the first `amount`. It creates a *new* variable that happens to share the name, calculated from the old one, and from that line onwards the name refers to the new variable. This is called **shadowing**, because the new variable casts a shadow over the old one.

Since the second amount is a new variable, nothing obliges it to resemble the first. In the figure it holds the number 12 and then, after a third let, the text twelve, which no assignment to a single variable could do, because an assignment must keep the type of value the variable was created with (the next lesson explains types properly). Shadowing is therefore the tool for building a value in stages, while mut suits a value that is updated again and again in place, such as a counter.

afterFigure.text: Each `let` leaves the earlier variable unchanged and merely out of reach by name, whereas an assignment overwrites the one variable that exists. When it is unclear which of the two a line is, check whether the line begins with **let**.

reveal.text: Both approaches print 7, so the choice between them depends on the job: shadowing when each step produces a fresh value, possibly of another type, and mut when one variable is updated repeatedly.

blocks.text: Here is a complete Rust program. The line `let apples = 3;` gives the name `apples` to the number 3, and from then on the name can be written wherever the number could, which is how the last line is able to add `apples` to `pears` without repeating either number.

Giving a value a name is the first thing nearly every program does, and Rust attaches a condition to it that most languages do not: a name keeps its value unless you say, on the line that creates it, that it may change. A reader can then tell from that one line which names might change later, and can rule out the others when something goes wrong. The same condition is the reason the compiler will sometimes refuse a program that looks perfectly reasonable.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a program that prints values, and say which of its variables may change.

recap.keyIdea: A name made with `let` keeps its value unless it was made with `let mut`, and `println!` fills its braces with the values or names you give it.

blocks.text: A Rust program starts at `fn main`, and **println!** fills each pair of braces with the next value, or with a name written inside the braces. A name created with **let** keeps its value, and only one created with **let mut** may be assigned a new one later, whereas a second `let` with the same name makes a *new* variable and leaves the old one untouched.

For a rejected assignment, rustc's message ends with the repair itself, so running the program is the quickest way to find out what is wrong with it. A name that never needs to change should be left without `mut`, because the missing word tells every later reader that its value can be trusted, and a [[shadowing|A second let that reuses a name and creates a new variable. Met earlier in this lesson.]] `let` is the way to build a value in stages when each stage is a new variable.

lessons.title: Types and functions

lead.text: Every value in a Rust program has a **type**, which says what kind of value it is and therefore what can be done with it. Numbers come in two families that are used constantly. The whole numbers, written with no decimal point, have types such as **i32**, a 32-bit integer that holds any whole number from about −2 billion to +2 billion, and the numbers with a decimal point have types such as **f64**, a 64-bit floating-point number. When you write a number and nothing else in the program says which type it has, Rust chooses `i32` for a whole number and `f64` for a number with a decimal point.

The distinction matters most for division. When both numbers are whole, the result is whole as well: Rust divides, discards the remainder and keeps the quotient, so 9 / 4 is 2 and not 2.25. Writing both numbers with a decimal point, as in 9.0 / 4.0, makes them f64 values, and the division keeps its fraction.

afterFigure.text: The figure prints both results side by side. The whole-number result is not 2.25 rounded: the remainder is simply dropped, so that `9 / 4` and `11 / 4` both give 2. A decimal point therefore changes the answer and not merely its appearance, because **9 and 9.0 are values of different types**.

reveal.text: Only the numbers changed. The name, the division and the `println!` stayed as they were, because the type of the result follows from the types of the numbers divided.

lead.text: A type can be written after a variable's name with a colon, as in price: f64.

reveal.text: Rust leaves the conversion to you, because a silent change between whole and decimal numbers could alter a result without leaving any sign in the code. The next screen shows the one word that makes the conversion explicit.

lead.text: To combine a whole number with a decimal one, you convert one of them, and the word **as** does so: `total as f64` takes the whole number held in `total` and produces the same number as an `f64`. The variable `total` is unchanged, since `as` makes a converted value and does not alter its source, and the new value can then be used in any calculation that needs an `f64`.

In the figure the whole number 9 is converted before the division, which is why the result keeps its fraction. The conversion belongs to total alone, because as binds more tightly than /: the line is read as (total as f64) / 2.0, a decimal divided by a decimal, and no mixing is left for the compiler to object to.

afterFigure.text: Conversion in the other direction is also possible, but it can lose something. Writing `9.7 as i32` gives 9, because the part after the decimal point is discarded and not rounded, whereas converting a whole number to `f64` keeps its value. **The word as marks the place in a program where you decide which of these you want.**

lead.text: The programs so far have contained one function, `main`. You write others with the same word `fn`, followed by a name, a list of **parameters** in brackets, and an arrow and a **return type** before the braces. In `fn double(n: i32) -> i32`, the function `double` takes one parameter, `n`, which must be an `i32`, and the arrow says that it hands back an `i32`. Every parameter and the result have their types written out in this way, because Rust does not guess the types at the edges of a function.

The body is the code between the braces, and the value that the function returns is simply its last line, written *without* a semicolon. In the figure that line is `n * 2`, so `double(21)` is 42, and `main` stores the value in `result` before printing it. A function is called by writing its name with the values to use for its parameters, and each call runs the body again with the parameters set to those values.

afterFigure.text: The first line of a function can be read as a contract: it says what must be supplied and what will come back, and the compiler checks every call against it. A call that supplies an f64 to double, or that treats its result as text, is rejected before the program runs, which is the same strictness about types as on the earlier screens.

reveal.text: Both parameters here are i32 as well, which makes the answer easy to confuse with theirs, but a function could equally take two i32 values and return an f64.
The same body served two different prices. That is the purpose of a parameter: the calculation is written once, each call supplies its own value, and nothing has to be copied.

lead.text: Here is `double` again, with a semicolon added after `n * 2`.

reveal.text: A semicolon turns an expression into a *statement*, which is carried out and produces no value, so the body ends without an `i32` to return. rustc reports that it expected an `i32` and found `()`, the empty value, points at the semicolon and suggests removing it.

lessons.nextAction: Write your own programs in the Rust projects.

blocks.text: A calculator divides 7 by 2 and shows 3.5. Whether a Rust program does the same depends on the kind of number it is dividing, because a whole number such as 7 and a number with a decimal point such as 7.0 are values of different **types**, and the type decides what an operation on them means.

Rust keeps track of types more strictly than most languages do, and that strictness is what lets a function state exactly what it needs and what it hands back. The compiler checks every call against that statement, so a program that mixes the two kinds of number carelessly is refused before it runs and not after it has produced a wrong answer.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose between whole and decimal numbers, and write a function that takes and returns typed values.

recap.keyIdea: Rust keeps whole numbers and decimals apart, and a function returns its last expression, so a semicolon there turns the result into nothing.

blocks.text: Rust treats whole numbers (**i32**) and decimals (**f64**) as different types, so `9 / 4` is 2 while `9.0 / 4.0` is 2.25, and a calculation that mixes the two is rejected until one side is converted with **as**. A function states the types it takes and the type it returns, and what it returns is its last expression, which is why a semicolon at the end of that line leaves the function with no value.
Together with printing, variables and mut from the previous lesson, these are the pieces that most small Rust programs are built from, and the Rust projects ask you to use them side by side.

lessons.title: Making decisions with if

lead.text: The program in the figure compares a temperature with 30 and prints one of two words. The part between **if** and the opening brace is the **condition**, which has to work out to a **bool**, a value that is either `true` or `false`; here it is the comparison `temperature > 30`. The block that follows runs when the condition is true, and the block after **else** runs when it is false, so exactly one of the two blocks is carried out each time.

Conditions are built from comparisons: `==` tests whether two values are equal, `!=` whether they differ, and `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` compare their order. Two conditions can be combined with `&&` (both must hold) and `||` (at least one must hold). Unlike C or Python, Rust accepts nothing but a `bool` in this position, so a number cannot stand in for "true if it is not zero".

afterFigure.text: With `temperature` set to 31, `31 > 30` is true and the program prints `hot`. Change the 31 to 25 and the `else` block runs instead. Because the comparison `>` leaves out equality, a temperature of exactly 30 would also print `mild`, which is the reason the boundary value is the one worth checking whenever you read a condition.

reveal.text: Changing `>=` to `>` in the condition would make the program print `child` instead, because `18 > 18` is false. The two symbols agree on every age except 18 itself.

lead.text: Two blocks are not always enough. Writing **else if** and a new condition in place of a plain `else` adds a further test, and a chain can have as many of them as it needs. Rust works through the chain in order, runs the block belonging to the first condition that is true, and skips every test below it, so the order of the tests is part of what the program means.

The figure follows a score through the chain from the grade program on the next screen. Use the buttons to change the score and watch which tests are reached: a score of 95 passes the first test and never meets the others, whereas 70 fails both tests and falls through to the final **else**, which has no condition because it takes whatever is left.

afterFigure.text: That order matters whenever the conditions overlap. A score of 95 is also at least 80, but the chain never asks, because the test for 90 came first and was already true. If the two tests were written the other way round, every score of 80 or more would receive a B.

reveal.text: Each branch is a bare string with no semicolon, and the whole chain is the last expression of the body, so no return keyword is needed.

lead.text: Most languages treat `if` as a statement that does something and produces nothing. In Rust an `if` with an `else` is an *expression*, which means that it works out to a value like `6 * 7` does, and that value can be given a name. A line such as `let kind = if n % 2 == 0 { "even" } else { "odd" };` runs the test and gives `kind` the text from whichever block was chosen, so no assignment appears inside the blocks.

A block's value is its last expression, written without a semicolon. That is why the blocks contain just "even" and "odd", and it is the same rule that gave a function its return value in the last lesson. The figure shows the two blocks feeding one slot, the value of the if, and the buttons show why Rust requires the blocks to agree: the slot gets a single type when both blocks have it, and none otherwise.

afterFigure.text: The same idea explains why a function body can be nothing but an if chain, as in describe. The chain is the last expression, so its value is the function's result, and a branch that ended in a semicolon would instead produce () and fail to match the others.

lead.text: Run the figure's program and rustc refuses it with **error[E0308]**, a mismatched types error. The first block gives the integer 1 and the second gives the text `"one"`, and a variable cannot be an integer on one path and text on the other, because Rust fixes the type of every variable before the program runs. The message marks both blocks, the first with *expected because of this*, since it was the first block that settled what the type should be.

Two related faults produce related messages. Using a bare number as the condition, as in `if count { ... }`, gives E0308 as well, with `bool` expected and an integer found. And an `if` with no `else` cannot be used as a value, because the missing branch would give `()`, the type of nothing, and no integer matches it; rustc reports that one as **E0317**. In each case the repair is to make every piece the same type: compare the number with something to get a `bool`, or add an `else` block of the same type as the first.

blocks.text: The expression `if n % 2 == 0 { n / 2 } else { n * 2 }` is a number: `n / 2` when `n` is even and `n * 2` when it is odd. In many languages an `if` only decides which lines of code run, but in Rust it has a value, as `6 * 7` does, and can sit on the right of a `let`, which is what is meant by calling an `if` an **expression**.

That one fact explains two rules that look arbitrary at first, namely that the test after if has to be a plain yes or no and that both branches have to give the same kind of value. It also lets a decision be written directly as the value it produces, so that no variable has to be created first and filled in afterwards.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write if, else if and else, use an if as a value, and say why rustc rejects a condition that is not a bool.
intro.whyItMatters: Almost every useful program makes a decision, and in Rust the decision is also a value.

recap.keyIdea: An if chooses one block by a bool condition and has the value of the block it ran, so every block must have the same type.

blocks.text: A condition built from comparisons has to be a **bool**, and an else-if chain tests from the top and runs only the first block whose test is true. The value of an `if` is the value of the block that ran, which is why you can put one on the right of `let` or at the end of a function.
That value needs a single type, so a mismatch between blocks gives E0308, and an if used as a value without an else gives E0317.

lessons.title: Repeating work with loops and ranges

lead.text: The keyword **loop** repeats its block without end, which is a useful property only because the block can contain a **break**, the statement that leaves the loop at once and carries on with the line after it. In the figure a counter is raised by 1 on every pass, the pass number is printed, and an `if` inside the body breaks when the counter reaches 3, so the body runs three times before `done` is printed.

Because a `loop` is an expression just as an `if` is, a `break` may hand a value out with it. Writing `let found = loop { ... break p; };` gives `found` the value that was named after the `break`, and this is the form of `loop` to use whenever a search stops at the first thing it finds.

afterFigure.text: A loop that never reaches its break runs until the program is stopped, so before running one, check that something in the body moves the program toward the break. The counter in the figure does that by growing, and the break tests the value that it reaches.

reveal.text: Changing the 100 to 300 would make the loop go on for one more pass and hand out 729.

lead.text: When the number of repetitions depends on a value that changes, a **while** loop is often clearer than a `loop` with a `break` in it, because the condition stands at the top where a reader looks first. Rust tests the condition before every pass, runs the body if it is true, and moves on as soon as it is false, so a body can run zero times if the condition starts out false.

The program in the figure halves a number until nothing is left to halve. The condition `n > 1` is checked at the top of each pass, the body halves `n` with `n /= 2` and counts the step, and after six passes `n` has fallen to 1 and the test fails. Since both integers and the division are whole, `25 / 2` is 12 and the remainder is dropped, which is the integer division from the last lesson at work.

afterFigure.text: The commonest mistake with `while` is a body that never changes anything that the condition reads. Had the line `n /= 2` been left out, `n` would stay at 100, the condition would stay true, and the program would never print.

reveal.text: The values of n were 100, 50, 25, 12, 6, 3 and 1. There are seven values and six steps between them.
The line `n -= 1;` is the part that makes the loop finish. Without it the program would print 3 without end.

lead.text: When you know the values to visit, a **for** loop is the shortest form: `for i in 1..4` sets `i` to each value in turn and runs the body once for each. The part after `in` is a **range**, which names the first value, two dots, and the end. Rust has no counting loop of the C kind with a start, a test and a step; `for` always walks through the values of a range or of something else that can supply them, and it makes the variable `i` itself.

The two dots leave out the end value, so `1..4` visits 1, 2 and 3. Writing **..=** includes it, so `1..=4` visits 1, 2, 3 and 4. The figure shows both on a number line, with an open dot where a range stops just short of a value and a filled dot where it includes it.

afterFigure.text: The number of values in a range follows from its ends. For `1..4` it is 4 - 1 = 3, and for `1..=4` it is 4 - 1 + 1 = 4, so counting the repetitions of a loop before running it only needs the two ends and a look at whether there is an equals sign. An empty range such as `1..1` has no values and the body never runs.

lead.text: A range is more than two ends, because methods called on it, functions written after a dot as in `.rev()`, change how it is visited. Writing `(1..=3).rev()` visits the same values backwards, 3, 2, 1, and `(0..10).step_by(3)` keeps every third value starting from the first, which are 0, 3, 6 and 9. The brackets round the range matter, since the method belongs to the whole range and not to its last number.
The program in the figure uses both. It also uses **print!**, the sibling of `println!` that leaves the line open, so that the values of one loop land on one line and a bare `println!()` closes it.

afterFigure.text: Counting repetitions works the same way as before. `step_by(3)` over `0..10` visits 0, 3, 6 and 9, that is four values, and the last of them is 9 because the next step would land on 12, beyond the end. The end of a range is a limit on the values, not a value that is guaranteed to appear.

reveal.text: The values are 0, 5, 10 and 15. The next one would be 20, which a range ending at 20 leaves out.

lead.text: A name lives from the line that creates it to the closing brace of the block it was made in, and the variable named after `for` is made inside the loop's block. When the loop finishes the block ends and the name goes with it, so the last line of the figure's program asks for a value that no longer exists. rustc reports **error[E0425]**, which says that it cannot find the value in this scope, and points at the use.

The repair is to create a variable before the loop, in the block that surrounds it, and to update it from inside. A variable made there is still alive after the loop has ended, and the body can reach it because an inner block may use the names of the blocks around it.

blocks.text: To find the first whole number whose square is above 50, you try 1, then 2, then 3, and check each square against 50 until one passes. Written out, that is the same step many times over, so a program writes it once, raising a counter by 1 and testing its square, and places it in a **loop** that repeats until a `break` leaves it carrying the number that passed.

Repeating a block is what lets the same few lines serve for ten values or for ten million, and the part that needs care is what stops it. Rust has three ways of writing a repetition, and they differ in exactly that: loop runs until a break inside it says so, while checks a condition before every pass, and for walks through values fixed in advance, such as the numbers from 1 to 10. Which one fits depends on what you know before the repetition starts, and a stopping rule written slightly wrong is the commonest reason a loop runs once too often or never ends.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose between loop, while and for, say how many values a range visits, and use break to stop or to hand out a value.
intro.whyItMatters: Counting repetitions correctly decides whether a program is off by one.

recap.keyIdea: `loop` repeats until `break`, `while` repeats as long as a `bool` holds, and `for` visits the values of a range, where `a..b` leaves out `b` and `a..=b` includes it.

blocks.text: Use **loop** when the program should stop at the first thing it finds and may carry that value out with `break`, **while** when a changing condition decides, and **for** when the values are known. A range `a..b` visits b - a values, and `a..=b` visits one more.
The variable of a for loop is gone after the loop, so a value needed afterwards has to be kept in a variable made before it.

lessons.title: Ownership and moves

lead.text: A **String** is text that can grow, and while it lives it holds a block of memory that has to be handed back to the system when the `String` is no longer needed. Rust settles who does the handing back by a rule with three parts: every value has an **owner**, which is the variable that holds it; a value has only one owner at a time; and when the owner goes out of **scope** the value is **dropped**, and its memory is released. `String::from("inner")` creates a `String` from the text, and `let` makes the variable the owner.

The figure has two variables in two blocks. The variable `inner` is created inside the inner pair of braces, so it goes out of scope at the closing brace and its `String` is dropped there, whereas `outer` lives until the end of `main`. Nothing in the program says *when* to `free` the memory; the closing brace does it, which is why Rust needs no garbage collector and no call to free.

afterFigure.text: The second part of the rule is the one with consequences. If two variables could own the same String, both would try to release the same memory when they went out of scope. Rust prevents that by allowing a value just one owner, and the next screens look at what happens to the old owner when a value is given to a new one.

lead.text: A move is needed only when copying would be expensive or unsafe, and the types that fit in a fixed few bytes need neither. An integer, a decimal number, a **bool** and a **char** are all small enough to be copied bit by bit, and Rust does so whenever one is assigned or passed. The name on the right of `let b = a;` keeps its value, and `b` gets a second one, so the program in the figure adds 5 and 5.

These types are marked as **Copy**, and a type is either `Copy` or it is not. The ones that own memory they must free, `String` and `Vec` among them, are never `Copy`, since two owners would both release it. When the compiler complains about a moved value, the first thing to look at is the type of the variable.

The decision follows from a rule: every value has exactly one **owner**, which is the variable that holds it, and when the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped and its memory released. The compiler checks the rule before the program runs, which is why Rust needs no garbage collector and leaves no dangling memory, and why it can refuse a program that uses a value after it has gone.

lessons.title: References and borrowing

lead.text: Passing a `String` to a function moves it, and the last lesson ended with the awkward fixes of returning the value or cloning it. A **reference** removes the need for either: writing **&name** makes a value that points at `name` without owning it, and handing that to a function **borrows** the `String` for the length of the call. The function declares what it expects as `fn length(s: &String) -> usize`, where `&String` means a reference to a `String` and `usize` is the unsigned integer type Rust uses for lengths and indexes, and the caller writes `length(&name)`.

When the call returns, the borrow is over and `name` still owns the text, which is why the last line of the program in the figure can print it. The function could read the text through `s`, using `s.len()`, but it never became the owner, so it has nothing to drop and nothing to give back.

afterFigure.text: A reference is a view of the same value and not a copy of it. That fact explains both its efficiency, since no text is copied, and its limits, which make up the rest of this lesson.

reveal.text: Because total only borrowed the Vec, the caller can use it again straight after the call, which the version that took the Vec by value would not allow.

lead.text: A shared reference only allows reading. To let a function change a value, you lend it with **&mut**, written at the call as `add_one(&mut n)` and in the signature as `n: &mut i32`. Two things have to agree for this to compile: the variable has to be declared with `let mut`, since you are giving permission for it to change, and the borrow has to be `&mut`, since you are giving permission to the function.

Inside `add_one`, `n` is a reference, and the number it points at is reached with the **dereference** operator `*`. The line `*n += 1` reads as *add 1 to what n points at*, and the effect is on the caller's variable. In the figure the first `show` call prints 10, `add_one` then raises the variable to 11, and the second `show` call prints that. The two `show` calls use `&` because they only read.

reveal.text: The change is made on the caller's variable. Had bump taken n: i32 and added 1 to its own copy, the program would have printed 5.

lead.text: Rust allows two kinds of borrow at the same time only in one combination. Any number of shared references may exist together, because reading through all of them cannot interfere. But a **mutable** reference must be the only reference of any kind, since a value that is being changed through one name cannot safely be read or changed through another.

The program in the figure takes two `&mut` references to `names` and then uses both. rustc stops at the second one with **error[E0499]**, which means that the value was borrowed as mutable more than once at a time, and marks three things: the first borrow, the second borrow, and the later use of the first that shows that the two overlap. The same rule, with one shared and one mutable reference, gives **E0502**.

afterFigure.text: These rules are checked before the program runs, and they rule out a whole group of faults, such as changing a list while another part of the program is walking through it, that other languages leave to discipline.

Permission is therefore needed at both ends, in the variable and in the borrow, and the compiler checks each one.

blocks.text: In the line `let r = &s;`, the `&` makes `r` a **reference** to the `String` `s`: a second name that can read the text but does not own it. Because `s` is still the owner, both names can be printed afterwards, which an ordinary assignment would not allow, since that moves the String and leaves the old name unusable.

A reference removes most of the returning and cloning that ownership alone forces on you, because a function can borrow a value for the length of a call and leave it with its owner. Borrowing comes with a short set of rules about who may read and who may change a value at any moment, and those are the rules rustc applies to the programs it refuses.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to pass values by & and &mut, and name the borrow rule behind E0502, E0499 and E0596.
intro.whyItMatters: Borrowing is how Rust programs share data without copying it or giving it away.

recap.keyIdea: A reference borrows a value without owning it: any number of `&` references or exactly one `&mut` may exist at a time, and a borrow lasts until its last use.

blocks.text: **&x** borrows `x` for reading and **&mut x** borrows it for changing, which also needs `x` declared with `let mut`, and `*` reaches the value behind a reference. At any moment a value has many shared references or one mutable one, and rustc reports E0502 when the two kinds overlap, E0499 for two mutable references, and E0596 for a change that was never allowed.
Because a borrow ends at the last use of its reference, a conflict can often be removed by reordering lines.

lessons.title: Slices, String and &str

lead.text: An array holds a fixed number of values of one type, written between square brackets, and a part of it can be borrowed without copying anything. Writing **&a[1..4]** takes the range `1..4` that the last lessons used for loops, and applies it as an index: the result is a **slice**, a reference to the items at indexes 1, 2 and 3. Its type is written `&[i32]`, a reference to a run of `i32` values of no fixed length, and its length is the end minus the start, here 3.

The figure prints the slice with the debug format **{:?}**, which Rust provides for lists and many other types, so the three items appear in square brackets. The slice is a view of the array and not a copy: the array still owns the numbers, and the slice is a borrow that obeys the borrow rules of the last lesson.

afterFigure.text: Either end of the range may be left out. `&a[..2]` starts at the beginning, `&a[3..]` runs to the end, and `&a[..]` is the whole array. Leaving the end out is also the clearest way to say *the rest*, since it does not require the length to be known.

reveal.text: Indexing the slice at 1 reaches `a[3]`, because the slice starts at `a[2]`. The positions are relative to the start of the slice.

lead.text: Rust has two main types for text, and the difference is the one between an owner and a borrow. A **String** owns its characters and can grow; you met it in the lesson on ownership. A **&str**, read as *string slice*, is a borrowed view of text that someone else owns, and a quoted literal such as `"hello"` is always a `&str`, because its text lives inside the program itself. Taking a slice of a `String` with a range, as in `&s[0..5]`, gives a `&str`, which the figure shows as a bracket over cells 0 to 4 of eleven.

The practical rule follows from this. A function that only reads text should take **&str**, because a literal can be passed as it is and a `String` can be passed as `&name`, which Rust converts automatically. A function taking `&String` would refuse the literal. A function should take a `String` only when it needs to own the text.

afterFigure.text: The slice records where its text starts and how long it is. In the second view of the figure the range is 6..11, and the text stays where it is: only the bracket moves.

lead.text: Python lets you write `s[0]` for the first letter, and the same line in Rust is an error. The figure's program asks for `s[0]` of a `String` and is refused with **error[E0277]**, which says that the type `str` cannot be indexed by an integer. The reason is how Rust stores text. A `String` is a sequence of bytes in the encoding called **UTF-8**, in which each character takes between one and four bytes, so the n-th byte is not always the n-th character, and a program that took it could land in the middle of a character.

Rust has you say which of the two you mean. `s.chars()` gives the characters one by one, so `s.chars().nth(0)` is the first character and `s.chars().count()` is how many there are, while `s.bytes()` gives the raw bytes. A range slice, such as `&s[0..5]`, is allowed, because it names byte positions explicitly, and if the range cuts through the middle of a character the program stops at run time with a *panic*, an immediate halt with an error message.

lead.text: The length of a piece of text depends on what you count. The method **len()** counts bytes, which is what the `String` occupies in memory, whereas **chars().count()** counts characters. For plain English letters the two agree, because each takes one byte. A character from another script takes more: each of the two characters in the word of the figure takes three bytes, so the word has 6 bytes and 2 characters.

The second line of the program takes the first character with `chars().take(1)` and gathers it into a new `String` with `collect()`, the usual way to turn a string of characters back into text. Counting letters, vowels or words should be done with `chars()`, and a length that is used to slice should be a length in bytes.
A character is written with single quotation marks, as in `c == 'a'`.

reveal.text: Counting characters with `chars()` works for any text, including text whose characters take several bytes.

lead.text: A slice is a borrow, so it is subject to the rules from the last lesson. In the figure, `word` is a slice of `s`, and `s.clear()` empties the `String` while `word` is still waiting to be printed. If that were allowed, `word` would point at text that no longer existed, and rustc therefore refuses the program with **E0502**: `s` is borrowed as immutable by the slice and as mutable by `clear`.

The repair is the one for any E0502, which is to let the slice finish before the change is made. Printing word before the call to clear leaves the same two lines in the opposite order, and the program compiles. The slice protects you, in this way, from the class of fault in which a position kept from before a change no longer matches the changed text.

blocks.text: The expression `&text[0..5]` takes the bytes at positions 0 to 4 of `"hello world"`, which spell the word hello, and it copies none of them: the result is a **slice**, a reference to part of the original text that records where the part starts and how long it is. Most languages build a fresh piece of text for the word and copy its characters into it, so a view of the original costs less.

The same kind of view serves for parts of arrays and parts of text, and it is why a function that only reads text can accept a literal and a String alike. It also explains two oddities that surprise newcomers, namely that Rust has two string types and that a string cannot be indexed by position.

lessons.title: Structs and methods

lead.text: Two related numbers, such as the width and height of a rectangle, are easier to keep together than to pass about separately. A **struct** gives them a shared name and a name each. The definition lists the **fields** with their types, and a value of the struct is built by writing the struct's name and then a value for every field. In the figure, `Rect` has the two fields `w` and `h`, and `r` is a `Rect` whose `w` is 30 and `h` is 50.

A field is read by writing the value, a dot and the field's name, so `r.w` is 30 and `r.h` is 50, and `r.w * r.h` is the area. A struct is a type like `u32` or `String`, which means that it can be a parameter, a return value or a field of another struct, and the compiler checks that every use agrees with the definition.

reveal.text: Changing one number in the line that builds r changes the answer, and no other line needs to change.

lead.text: Struct values obey the rule for variables that you met in the first lesson. A variable made with plain `let` cannot be changed, and a struct made with plain `let` cannot have any of its fields changed either; there is no way to mark a single field as changeable. The program in the figure tries to give `p.x` a new value and is refused with **error[E0594]**, which says that `p` cannot be assigned to because it is not declared `mut`.

The repair is the same one word as before, `let mut p`, and then each field can be assigned with `p.x = 5`. The choice is made for the whole value, so a struct whose fields should change at different times is still declared `mut` as a whole.

lead.text: A function that works on a `Rect` belongs next to the `Rect`, and Rust puts it there with an **impl** block. A function in the block whose first parameter is **&self** is a **method**: `self` is the value the method was called on, and `&self` borrows it, so the method can read `self.w` and `self.h` and the caller keeps the value. A method is called by writing the value, a dot and the method's name, as in `r.area()`.

The figure shows what the dot means. The call `r.area()` is shorthand for `Rect::area(&r)`, in which the value is passed as the first argument and the reference is made for you, and inside the method `self` is that reference. Because the method only borrowed `r`, the call can be repeated as often as you like.

lead.text: Which form of `self` a method takes decides what it may do with the value, and it uses the ownership rules from the last three lessons. **&self** borrows the value for reading. **&mut self** borrows it for changing, and the variable has to be `let mut`, as with any mutable borrow. A plain **self** takes ownership, which consumes the value, and is for methods that turn a value into something else. Most methods use `&self` or `&mut self`.

A function in an `impl` block with no `self` is called an **associated function**, and it is called with the type's name and two colons, as in `Counter::new()`. The usual use is a **constructor**: `new` builds a value, and **Self** inside an `impl` block is a short name for the type being implemented. In the figure, `Counter::new()` starts the count at 0, `increment` adds 1 through `&mut self`, and `get` reads it through `&self`.

lead.text: The braces in `println!` print a value in the ordinary form that a person would expect, and a struct has no such form until you write one, so `println!("{}", p)` is an error. Rust offers a second form for the programmer's own use, called **Debug**, which every type can have by writing **#[derive(Debug)]** on the line above its definition. With it, `{:?}` prints the value on one line with the field names, and `{:#?}` spreads it over several lines.

The program in the figure builds a Point and prints it both ways, and then prints the sum of its fields to show that the ordinary use of fields is unchanged. Debug output is meant for checking what a value holds while you write a program, and not for showing to a user.

blocks.text: A rectangle is two numbers, a width and a height, and a program that handles many of them soon has pairs of numbers passing from function to function with nothing but a variable name to say which is the width. A **struct** keeps the two under one name, and a function written beside it lets the rectangle answer for itself, so that `r.area()` asks a rectangle for its area where `area(w, h)` would need the numbers passed in separately.

Together these let a program speak about its own subject in its own words, and they bring the ownership rules of the last three lessons into the design of every function you write, since each function that works on a value has to say whether it reads the value, changes it or takes it over.

lessons.title: Enums and match

lead.text: Some values are best described as a choice from a short list: a coin is a penny, a nickel, a dime or a quarter, and nothing in between. An **enum** names that list. Each name inside the braces is a **variant**, and a value of the type is one of them, written with the enum's name, two colons and the variant, as in `Coin::Dime`. A variable of type `Coin` holds exactly one variant at a time.

The **match** expression takes a value and a list of **arms**, each an arm with a pattern on the left of **=>** and a result on the right. Rust compares the value with the patterns from the top and runs the first arm that fits, and since `match` is an expression, the value of that arm is the value of the whole `match`. In the figure, `value_in_cents` ends in a `match` whose four arms give 1, 5, 10 and 25, and passing `Coin::Dime` selects the third.

afterFigure.text: Only the arm that fits runs. Unlike the switch of some languages, a match does not carry on into the arm below, so no break is needed and no arm can run by accident.

reveal.text: The function returns a different number for each variant, and nothing in the call changes except the value passed in.

lead.text: The figure's `match` handles two of the three suits, and rustc refuses the program with **error[E0004]**, which says that the patterns are *not exhaustive* and names the one that is not covered, here `Suit::Clubs`. Because a value of the type may be any of its variants, a `match` over it has to say what happens for each, and the compiler checks this, so a forgotten case becomes an error you read and not a fault you meet later.

This also pays off when a program changes. If you add a fourth suit to the enum, every `match` over `Suit` that does not cover it stops compiling, and the compiler's list of errors is a list of the places that need a decision. A single arm written **_** matches everything that earlier arms did not, and is the right tool when the remaining cases really do share one answer.

afterFigure.text: The wildcard has a cost that is easy to overlook: a match that ends in _ keeps compiling after a variant is added, and so the compiler no longer points out the places where the new variant should be handled.

lead.text: The variants of `Coin` were only names, but a variant can also hold values. Each variant of `Message` in the figure holds something different: `Quit` holds nothing, `Move` holds two numbers with the names `x` and `y`, as a struct would, and `Write` holds one `String` in brackets. A value is built from the variant and its data, as in `Message::Move { x: 2, y: 5 }`, and Rust keeps track of which variant it is as well as the data inside.

The patterns of a `match` have the same shapes. The arm `Message::Move { x, y }` fits a `Move` value and creates the names `x` and `y` for the data inside it, so the arm's code can use them, and `Message::Write(text)` does the same for the `String`. Choose a case in the figure to see which arm lights up and what it prints. The data is available only inside the arm that matched, since it exists only for that variant.

lead.text: Patterns are not limited to variants. A literal such as 0 matches that value, a range such as **1..=9** matches every value from 1 to 9, and an arm can carry a **guard**, an extra condition written with `if` after the pattern. The arm `n if n < 0` binds the value to `n` and runs only when the guard is true. The arms are tried from the top, so the order matters, and the final **_** takes whatever is left.

The function in the figure sorts a number into four groups with a guard, a literal, a range and a wildcard. Because the first arm to fit wins, the groups do not overlap even though a number such as 5 could be said to satisfy several conditions in the abstract. The match must still be exhaustive: here the wildcard guarantees that, since the earlier patterns cannot cover every integer on their own.

reveal.text: The number 9 is the end of a range, which is where an off-by-one in a pattern would show.

lead.text: Methods work on enums as they do on structs, through an `impl` block. A method that takes **self** by value consumes the variant and can return a different one, which is how the figure's `turn_right` moves a `Direction` one step round. Its body is a `match` on `self` with one arm for each variant, so the compiler checks that every direction has a next one.

The same shape serves to describe a state that moves through a fixed cycle, such as a traffic light or the stage of an order. The enum names the states, each method names an operation, and the matches inside the methods are the only places that need to know which variant is which.

reveal.text: `next` takes `self` by value, so the variable in `main` is given the new light each time: `light = light.next();`.

blocks.text: A coin in a program can be a penny, a nickel, a dime or a quarter and nothing else, and Rust lets you say exactly that: an **enum** called `Coin` whose value is always one of four named variants. A `match` then takes a `Coin` and gives the amount that goes with each kind, with one arm for each variant and no `if` and no comparison of numbers.

A value that is exactly one of several kinds is something nearly every program needs, and other languages stand in for it with integer codes, strings or null checks, none of which the compiler can check. Because Rust knows every variant, it can tell you when a match leaves one out, so a forgotten case becomes an error you read and not a fault you meet later.

recap.keyIdea: An enum is exactly one of its variants, which may carry data, and a match covers every variant and gives the value of the first arm that fits.

blocks.text: An **enum** lists the variants a value can be, and a **match** chooses an arm for each of them, binding any data a variant carries, so the compiler can tell you with E0004 when a variant is missing. Literals, ranges, guards and the wildcard `_` give a `match` finer control, and the first arm that fits is the one that runs.
Methods in an impl block, usually matching on self, say what each variant does.

lessons.title: Option: a value that may be missing

lead.text: Many operations might not have an answer: the item at an index that does not exist, the first character of an empty string, the result of dividing by zero. Languages with a null value let such an answer be absent without saying so, and a program that forgets to check meets the absence later, often in a place far from its cause. Rust has no null. It has a standard enum, **Option<T>**, with two variants: **Some(value)** holds a value of type `T`, and **None** holds nothing.

Because `Option<i32>` and `i32` are different types, a function that returns `Option<i32>` forces its caller to deal with both cases. The figure draws one of each: `Some(7)` carries the number, `None` carries nothing, and a `match` over the `Option` has an arm for each. The plain `i32` at the bottom is a different kind of thing, and the compiler will not let the two be mixed up.

afterFigure.text: `None` does not mean 0 or an empty string. It means that there is no value at all, and `Some(0)` is a perfectly good value that happens to be zero.

lead.text: The standard library returns an `Option` wherever a value may be absent: `get` for an item at an index, `last` for the final item, and many others. To use the result you take it apart with `match`, as in the previous lesson, with the arm `Some(n)` binding the value inside and the arm `None` saying what to do without one. In the figure, the loop asks the `Vec` for three indexes, and the `match` prints the item or the word `nothing`.

When only the `Some` case matters, the **if let** form says so directly: `if let Some(last) = nums.last() { ... }` runs the block with `last` bound to the value if there is one, and skips it otherwise. It is a `match` with the `None` arm left out, and Rust allows it because the program has stated that nothing needs to happen in that case. An `else` block can still be added for the other case.

steps.headline: An Option is not its value

lead.text: The program in the figure adds an `i32` to an `Option<i32>`, a mistake that a language with null would let through. rustc refuses it with **error[E0277]**, which says that the type `i32` cannot be added to `Option<i32>`. The same family of mistake appears as **E0308** when an `Option` is assigned to a variable declared as an `i32`, and as **E0369** when an operator such as `+` is applied to the `Option` on its own.

The message is not an obstacle to get around. The program has not yet said what the sum should be when the value is missing, and the compiler is asking. You answer by unpacking the Option with match, if let or one of the methods in the next screen, and the answer you choose is written in the program for every reader to see.

lead.text: When a missing value should simply be replaced, **unwrap_or(default)** is the shortest way to say so. It returns the value inside a `Some`, and the default for `None`, so the result is a plain value that can be added or printed. In the figure, `get(1)` is `Some(20)` and gives 20, and `get(5)` is `None` and gives 0. The method **copied()** comes first, because `get` returns an `Option` holding a reference to an item, and `copied` turns it into an `Option` holding the number itself.

A cousin of `unwrap_or` is **unwrap**, which returns the value inside a `Some` and, for `None`, stops the program at once with a message called a *panic*. It is useful in a short test or when you have already shown that the value is there, and it is a risk anywhere else. A program that unwraps whatever the compiler complains about has put back the null fault that `Option` was meant to remove.

afterFigure.text: The usual order of preference is `match` or `if let` when the two cases do different things, `unwrap_or` when a default makes sense, and `unwrap` only when `None` would be a mistake in the program itself.

lead.text: A function often needs a value before it can do anything useful, and the code that handles its absence is best kept short. The form **let Some(first) = v.first() else { ... };** tries the pattern on the left and, if it fits, binds `first` for the rest of the function. If it does not fit, the `else` block runs, and that block has to leave the function, here with `return`.

The figure shows two calls. For the list of two numbers the pattern fits and the function prints the first of them. For the empty list the pattern does not fit, so the else block prints empty and returns, and the lines below it are never reached. The benefit over a match is that the main work stays at the left margin and is not nested inside an arm.

reveal.text: A match needs both arms, so the program cannot print a missing number by accident, which would be the fault in a language with null.
Both arms had the type `Option<char>`, so the `match` as a whole did too, and the function's signature stayed honest about the empty string.

blocks.text: Asking a list of three numbers for the item at index 5 leaves nothing to return, and a language with a null value hands back a null that looks like any other result, so nothing marks the difference until a later line tries to use it. Rust answers with a value that says there is nothing, called **None**, and when the item does exist it answers with the item inside a wrapper, written `Some`, that says so.

The wrapper is part of the type, so a function that can fail to produce a value cannot be used as though it always did, and that one design decision removes a whole family of faults. Each use of such a result has to say what should happen when there is no value, and that answer is written in the program for every reader to see.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to return an Option from your own function, and unpack one with match, if let, unwrap_or and let-else.
intro.whyItMatters: Option makes a missing value a visible part of a function's type.

recap.keyIdea: `Option<T>` is `Some(value)` or `None` and is a different type from `T`, so a missing value must be handled with `match`, `if let`, `unwrap_or` or let-else.

blocks.text: A function that may have no answer returns **Option<T>**, and its caller takes the result apart with **match** or **if let**, replaces a missing value with **unwrap_or**, or leaves early with let-else. Using the `Option` as if it were the value inside is refused, with E0277, E0308 or E0369 according to the use.
unwrap stops the program on None, so use it only when None would itself be a bug.

lessons.title: Errors with Result and ?

lead.text: `Option` says that a value may be missing, but it cannot say why. When a function can fail for a reason that the caller may want to know, Rust uses a second standard enum, **Result<T, E>**. Its variant **Ok(value)** holds the value of type `T` when everything worked, and its variant **Err(error)** holds an error of type `E` when it did not. The method **parse** turns text into a number and is the usual first example, since text typed by a person may be anything.

The program in the figure parses two texts and prints what comes back with the debug format. The text `"12"` gives `Ok(12)`, and `"abc"` gives an `Err` holding a `ParseIntError`, a value that records the reason for the failure, here `InvalidDigit`. The `::<i32>` after `parse` tells it which type of number to produce, which it cannot work out for itself in this call.

afterFigure.text: An error in Rust is an ordinary value, returned from the function like any other. There are no exceptions that fly up the call stack unseen, so every place where a failure can occur is visible in the code.

reveal.text: The empty text is an error too, with its own message, because there are no digits to read.

lead.text: You take a `Result` apart in the same way as an `Option`, with a `match` whose arms bind the value inside each variant. In the figure the `Ok` arm prints the number and the `Err` arm prints the error `e`, which displays as a sentence from the standard library, such as *invalid digit found in string*. The debug format used for each text in the program prints it in quotation marks, which makes the empty text visible.

Both arms are required, as with any match, so a program that parses text has to say what happens when the text is bad. The Err arm could print a message, as here, supply a default value, or ask the user again, and the decision is made where the program knows what to do and not left to chance.

lead.text: A function with several steps that may each fail would need a match after every one, and the matches would soon bury the work. The **?** operator is the short form. Written after an expression that gives a `Result`, it does one of two things: for `Ok(value)` it produces the value, so the line goes on, and for `Err(e)` it returns that `Err` from the function immediately, so the lines below it never run.

In `add`, the first `?` gives `x` the number from the first text, the second gives `y` the number from the second, and `Ok(x + y)` wraps the sum. If either text is bad, `add` returns the `Err` of that parse and stops. The function's return type, `Result<i32, ParseIntError>`, is what makes this legal: the `Err` that `?` returns has to fit in it.

afterFigure.text: The second call in `main` shows the other path. `"three"` is not a number, so the second `?` returns the error and `add` gives back `Err(ParseIntError { kind: InvalidDigit })` without computing a sum.

lead.text: The figure follows add through its three lines. With both texts valid, each ? lets the Ok value through, the path runs down the function, and the last line builds the answer for the caller. Use the buttons to make the second parse fail: the first line still succeeds, the second line sends its Err out of the function along the side arrow, and the last line is never reached.

Seen this way, ? is the same as a match that has an arm for Ok that continues and an arm for Err that returns, written in one character. It does not hide the failure. The caller still receives an Err and must handle it, and the function's signature still tells every reader that it can fail.

lead.text: The error that `?` returns has to go somewhere, and it goes to the function's caller as the function's return value. The program in the figure uses `?` in `main`, whose return type is `()`, the unit type that means nothing, so there is no way to return an `Err` and rustc refuses it with **error[E0277]**: the `?` operator can only be used in a function that returns `Result` or `Option`.

There are two repairs. A `main` that should be able to fail can say so in its signature, `fn main() -> Result<(), ParseIntError>`, and finish with `Ok(())`, which the runtime reports as a failure exit if it receives an `Err`. Or the code that uses `?` can move into a helper function that returns a `Result`, with `main` handling the `Result` by a `match`, which is the pattern of the programs earlier in this lesson.

lead.text: Some failures cannot sensibly be handled by the code that called the function, and Rust gives those a different tool. **panic!** stops the program with a message, and **unwrap** and **expect** do the same when they meet an `Err` or a `None`. Use one when the failure shows a bug in the program itself, such as a position that the program's own logic guarantees is valid, because there is nothing for a caller to do and a clear stop is better than carrying on with wrong data.

For anything that can happen on a correct program, such as a mistyped number, a missing file or a closed connection, return a Result. The caller knows what it is for and can ask again, use a default or pass the failure on with ?. The figure puts the two cases side by side: an error that someone could cause belongs in a Result, and an error that only a mistake in the code could cause belongs in a panic.

blocks.text: Text typed by a person may be anything, so a call such as `"abc".parse::<i32>()` cannot always produce a number. In Rust it returns a **Result**, a value that is either `Ok` holding the number or `Err` holding the reason it failed, and a function that adds two pieces of text therefore has two chances to fail before it can give a sum.

A failure in Rust is an ordinary value that travels in a function's return type, which is the language's replacement for exceptions, and a single character, ?, is enough to pass it up the chain of calls. The code stays short while every point where something can fail remains visible, both in the function's signature and at the line that handles it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write a function that returns a Result, pass errors up with ?, and decide whether a failure should be an Err or a panic.
intro.whyItMatters: Real programs read input that can be wrong, and Result is how Rust keeps that failure visible.

recap.keyIdea: A function that can fail returns `Result<T, E>`, and `?` gives the `Ok` value or returns the `Err` at once, which works only where the return type can carry the error.

blocks.text: **Result<T, E>** is either `Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`, and a function that can fail says so in its return type. You take a `Result` apart with `match`, or pass the error up with **?**, which needs a function that itself returns a `Result` or `Option` and otherwise gives E0277.
Return an `Err` for failures that the caller can handle, such as bad input, and keep `panic!`, `unwrap` and `expect` for bugs.

lead.text: A fixed array cannot grow, and most programs need a list whose length is not known when they are written. The standard type for that is **Vec<T>**, a growable list in which every item has the type `T`. A `Vec` is built with the macro **vec![]** or with `Vec::new()` for an empty one, and it has to be declared `mut` before it can change. **push** adds an item at the end, and **len()** reports how many items there are.

**pop** removes the last item and returns it, but since an empty `Vec` has no last item, `pop` returns an `Option`, `Some(item)` or `None`, and the program in the figure prints it with the debug format. The `Vec` then has one item fewer, and the lengths and values on the three lines show the state after each step.

afterFigure.text: A Vec owns its items, so the ownership rules apply to it exactly as they did to a String: assigning it or passing it by value moves it, and a reference lets a function look at it without taking it.

reveal.text: The 4 was pushed and popped, so it never appears in the result. Only the 5 pushed afterwards is at the end.

lead.text: There are two ways to read an item of a `Vec`, and they differ in what they do when the position does not exist. **v[i]** gives the item itself, which is convenient, but a `Vec` of three items has no item at index 5 and the program stops with a panic. **v.get(i)** gives an `Option`, `Some(item)` when the position exists and `None` when it does not, and the program decides what to do.

The figure shows a `Vec` of three items and asks for index 5 in each way. Use `v[i]` where the position is certain to be valid, for instance inside a loop over `0..v.len()`, and `v.get(i)` wherever it comes from input or from a calculation that could go wrong.

lead.text: The ownership rules decide how a `for` loop may walk through a `Vec`. Writing **for w in &words** borrows the `Vec`, gives `w` as a reference to each item in turn, and leaves `words` usable afterwards. Writing **for x in &mut v** borrows it mutably, so that each `x` is a reference through which the item can be changed, as in `*x *= 2`. Writing **for w in words** with no `&`, as in the figure, moves the `Vec` into the loop, because the loop takes ownership of what it goes through.

That is why the figure's program is refused, with **error[E0382]** pointing at the use of `words` after the loop: the items were handed to the loop one by one, and the `Vec` was used up. rustc's suggestion is the repair, to iterate over `&words`. A loop that really should consume the `Vec` is rarer, and is written without the `&`.

lead.text: A `String` is a `Vec` of bytes that holds valid text, and it grows in the same way. **push** adds a single character and **push_str** adds a piece of text, so the `String` has to be declared `mut`. In the figure, the first three calls build `a-b` one piece at a time, and **format!** then makes a new `String` from a template, with the same braces as `println!`. It prints nothing itself and returns the `String`, which is why it is the usual way to join values into one piece of text.

The `+` operator also joins strings, as in `String::from("x") + "y"`, but it takes its left side by value and so uses it up, which makes `format!` easier to use when a piece of text is needed again. Whichever way a `String` is built, `len()` counts bytes, as in the lesson on slices.

reveal.text: The length is the three letters plus the two dashes. A loop that put a dash after each piece would have ended with a dash that no one wanted.

lead.text: Looking an item up by its position suits a list, and looking one up by a name suits a **HashMap<K, V>**, which stores a value of type `V` under each key of type `K`. **insert** adds a pair, and inserting a key that is already there replaces its value. **get** takes a key and returns an `Option`, `Some(value)` if the key is stored and `None` if not, and **contains_key** answers with a `bool`. The map has to be declared `mut` for `insert`, and the `HashMap` type has to be brought in with `use std::collections::HashMap;` at the top of the file.

In the figure, Ada is inserted twice, and the second insert replaces her 36 with 37. `get("Ada")` therefore gives `Some(37)`, `get("Grace")` gives `None`, and the map has two keys, Ada and Alan. Neither the keys nor the values are kept in any particular order.

Counting how often each word appears is the commonest use of a map, and the **entry** method is made for it. `counts.entry(word)` looks for the key, and **or_insert(0)** gives back a mutable reference to its count, after first inserting 0 if the key was absent. The line `*counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1` therefore starts every new word at 0 and adds 1 for every sighting, in one statement and without a separate check for the key.

A `HashMap` keeps its pairs in an unspecified order, and the order can differ from one run of the program to the next. For output that is the same every time, collect the keys into a `Vec` and sort it, as the figure does before printing the three counts. The sorted order here is alphabetical, one then three then two, and is unrelated to the order in which the words appeared.

reveal.text: The number of different words is the length of the map, because each key is stored once however often it was counted.
