blocks.text: A program that adds up the scores of however many players turn up cannot give each score a name in advance, since it does not know how many there will be. A **Vec** holds them: it starts empty, grows by one each time a value is pushed onto it, reports how many values it holds, and can be walked through with a loop to add them up.

Text that is built piece by piece and tables in which a value is found by a key have the same need, and the standard library supplies a type for each, `String` and `HashMap`. All three follow the ownership rules from earlier in the course, so the way a loop is written decides whether it borrows a collection or uses it up.

intro.whyItMatters: Almost every program keeps its data in one of these three types.

recap.keyIdea: `Vec` is a growable list, `String` is growable text, and `HashMap` finds values by key, and a `for` loop over `&v` borrows a collection while a loop over `v` uses it up.

blocks.text: A **Vec** grows with `push` and shrinks with `pop`, which returns an `Option`, and `v[i]` panics out of range while `v.get(i)` returns an `Option`. A `for` loop over `&v` borrows the collection, over `&mut v` borrows it for changing, and over `v` itself moves it.

A `String` grows with `push` and `push_str`, and `format!` builds a new one. A **HashMap** inserts, replaces, looks up with `get` and counts with `entry(key).or_insert(0)`, and its order is unspecified, so sort the keys before printing.

lessons.title: Traits and generics

lead.text: `Square` and `Rect` in the figure both have an area, and a program might well want to treat them alike. A shared name is not enough for that, because the compiler sees two unrelated methods. A **trait** gives the shared behaviour a name of its own: `trait Area` lists the signature `fn area(&self) -> f64` and no body. A type **implements** the trait with a block `impl Area for Square`, which supplies the body for that type, and a type that has no such block does not have the behaviour.

A trait holds only behaviour, with no fields, so the data stays in the structs: Square holds one side and Rect two. The same method name now means a different calculation for each type, and each call uses the body belonging to the type of the value in front of the dot. Everything that implements Area has an area method that returns an f64, and a function can rely on that.

Part of a trait's behaviour can often be written once in terms of the rest. In the figure, `Speak` requires one method, `name`, and provides `greet` with a body that builds a sentence from it. A type that implements `Speak` only has to write `name` to receive `greet` as well, as `Dog` does, and the default calls the Dog's own name through `self.name()`. A type may also write its own `greet` to replace the default, as `Cat` does.

The result is that the two calls print different lines from the same trait. The method `name` is **required**, since the trait gives no body for it, while `greet` is **provided**. Putting shared logic in a default body is how a trait avoids every implementer repeating it.

afterFigure.text: The types `Dog` and `Cat` are written `struct Dog;` and `struct Cat;`, structs with no fields, which suit a type that exists to carry behaviour.

reveal.text: Had Robot written its own greet, that one would have replaced the default, as Cat's did on the last screen.

lead.text: A function that finds the larger of two numbers should not need a second copy for decimals or characters. Writing **fn bigger<T>(a: T, b: T) -> T** declares a **type parameter** `T` in angle brackets, and the compiler produces a version of the function for each concrete type that the program uses. The function is written once, and nothing is slower at run time, because the specialised copies are made before the program runs.

The difficulty is that, inside the body, `T` could be anything, so the compiler knows nothing about it. The figure's body compares `a` and `b` with `>`, and rustc refuses it with **error[E0369]**: the binary operation `>` cannot be applied to type `T`. The repair is to promise something about `T`, and the next screens do that with a **trait bound**.

lead.text: A bound is written after the type parameter, as in `fn largest<T: PartialOrd + Copy>(v: &[T]) -> T`. **PartialOrd** is the trait behind `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`, so the body may compare two items. **Copy** lets an item be duplicated out of the slice, as `let mut best = v[0];` does, without moving it from the slice. The plus sign joins the two requirements, and a caller can use the function only with types that meet both.

The program in the figure calls `largest` three times, with integers, decimals and characters, and the compiler checks the bound for each. The longer the list of bounds, the harder the line is to read, so Rust offers a **where** clause that moves them after the signature, and **impl Trait** as a short form for a parameter, as in `fn show(x: impl Display)`. All three mean the same thing.

reveal.text: A version that started best at 0 would have returned 0, which is not in the list, so starting from an item is part of what makes it correct.
Only the comparison changed, and the bounds stayed the same, because both functions need the same two abilities of T.

lead.text: A struct with a type parameter, **Pair<T>**, holds two values of the same type `T`, so that `Pair { a: 3, b: 7 }` is a pair of integers and `Pair { a: 'q', b: 'c' }` a pair of characters. The `impl` block repeats the parameter, as `impl<T: PartialOrd + Copy> Pair<T>`, and the bound is stated there because only the method `bigger` needs it: a `Pair` of any type can exist, and the method is available only when `T` can be compared and copied.

In the figure, bigger compares the two fields and returns the larger, which is a copy of one of them. For the integers that is 7, and the same method works unchanged for any other type that meets the bound.

Trait bounds work in the same way for your own traits. The function `print_area<T: Area>` accepts any type that implements `Area`, so it can be called with a `Square` or a `Rect`, and inside it the call `shape.area()` is allowed because the bound promises it. A type that has no `impl` for the trait is refused at the call, with error E0277 and a message that the trait is not implemented for it.

Use the buttons in the figure to try three types. `Square` and `Rect` each have an `impl`, so the call compiles, and a `Circle` that was never given one is turned away. The function does not need to know how many types will implement `Area` or what they are, and a new type becomes usable with `print_area` the moment it implements the trait.

blocks.text: A square and a rectangle can each work out their own area with a method called area, but the shared name is only a coincidence, and the compiler cannot make use of it: a function that should accept a square or a rectangle, and nothing that lacks an area, has no way of saying so. With ten kinds of shape, every function that works on a shape would need ten versions.

Rust removes the repetition in two parts. A **trait** gives a behaviour, such as having an area, a name of its own so that types can share it, and a **generic** function or struct is written once for any type that has the behaviour. The compiler still checks every use before the program runs.

recap.keyIdea: A trait names behaviour that types opt into, and a generic function or struct is written once for any type whose bounds promise the operations the body uses.

blocks.text: A **trait** lists method signatures, may give some a default body, and is implemented for a type with `impl Trait for Type`. A generic function declares a type parameter, and its body may use only what the **bounds** promise, so comparing two values needs `T: PartialOrd` and printing one needs `T: Display`.
Without the bound, rustc reports E0369 for an operator and E0277 for a missing trait, and each message names the bound to add.

lessons.title: Lifetimes in signatures

lead.text: A reference is a pointer, and a pointer is only useful while the thing it points to still exists. In the program in the figure, `r` is declared outside an inner block, `x` is created inside it, and `r` is set to `&x`. At the closing brace `x` goes out of scope and is dropped, but `r` is used on the next line, when it would point at a value that is gone. Languages without a check call that a dangling pointer, and its use is a source of crashes and security faults. Rust refuses to compile it, with **error[E0597]**: `x` does not live long enough.

The check works by giving every reference a **lifetime**, the stretch of the program during which it is valid, and comparing it with the stretch for which the value lives. The reference `r` is used from line 3 to line 6, and the value `x` lives only until the block ends on line 5, so the first stretch is not inside the second. rustc names both and marks the line where `x` is dropped.

A reference returned from a function has to borrow from something that outlives the call, and the only candidates are the references that were passed in. With a single input that is obvious. The function in the figure takes two, `x` and `y`, and returns one of them depending on their lengths, so the result may borrow from either, and rustc cannot tell from the signature how long the caller may use it. It reports **error[E0106]**: missing lifetime specifier, and offers a repair.

The compiler checks the *caller's* code against the signature, and does not read the body to find out. That is why the signature itself has to say how the result's lifetime relates to the inputs: every caller must be able to know, from the signature alone, how long the result stays valid.

lead.text: A **lifetime annotation** is a name that starts with an apostrophe, declared in angle brackets after the function's name and attached to references with `&'a`. The signature `fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str` says that `x`, `y` and the result all share the lifetime `'a`. In practice `'a` stands for the part of the program in which both inputs are alive, so the result is valid there and no longer.

An annotation describes a relation that already exists. It does not make any value live longer, and it changes nothing about what the function does: the body in the figure is the same one that produced E0106, and the program now prints rust, the longer of the first pair, and ab, the first of the equal-length pair. What the annotation changes is what the compiler can check at each call.

The figure is a timeline of one call. The bars for x and y show when each input is alive, and the dashed lines mark the part where both are, which is what 'a means for this call. The bar for the result must fit inside that part. In the first view the result is still in use after y has gone, so the part that sticks out is drawn in red, and rustc would refuse the call. In the second the result ends while both inputs are alive, and the call is accepted.

This is the whole mechanism. Each call has its own 'a, taken from the actual lifetimes of the arguments, and the compiler tests whether the way the result is used fits inside it. When a program fails with E0597 and the lifetimes were annotated correctly, the fault is that a value was dropped too early, and the fix is to let it live longer, usually by declaring it in an outer block.

lead.text: The `first_word` function of the lesson on slices took a `&str` and returned a `&str`, and it needed no annotation. The compiler applies the rules of **lifetime elision** before it complains: if a function has exactly one input reference, the result is given that lifetime, and if it has `&self` or `&mut self`, the result is given the lifetime of `self`. The signature in the figure is therefore read as `fn first_word<'a>(s: &'a str) -> &'a str`, with the `'a` written in for you.

When the rules cannot settle it, as with two input references and no self, the compiler asks, which is the E0106 of the earlier screen. The rules save typing, and they are not a different mechanism: every reference in a signature has a lifetime, and the annotation only makes it visible.

No annotation can rescue a reference to something that does not outlive the call. In the figure, `make` creates a `String`, and returns `&s`, a reference to it, but `s` is dropped at the closing brace of `make`, and the caller would receive a reference to nothing. rustc reports **error[E0515]**: cannot return reference to local variable, and says that the reference is to data owned by the current function.

The repair is to give the caller the value and not a view of it. Returning the String itself, with the return type String, moves ownership to the caller, who may keep it as long as it likes. A function returns a reference only when the reference points at something that was passed in, or at something that lives for the whole program.

lead.text: A struct usually owns its fields, but it can hold a reference too, and the reference then needs a lifetime. In the figure, `struct Excerpt<'a> { part: &'a str }` declares the parameter `'a` after the name and uses it on the field. The function `first_sentence` takes the text with lifetime `'a` and returns an `Excerpt<'a>`, which says that the excerpt borrows from the text it was given.

The consequence is that an Excerpt cannot outlive the String that it was cut from. In main, e is used while novel is still alive, so the program is accepted and prints the first sentence. Moving the printing after novel's block would be refused with E0597, as in the first screen. The struct costs no copy of the text, and the lifetime is the price.

blocks.text: A reference to a number x is only useful while x exists. If x is made inside a pair of braces and the reference is used after them, nothing looks wrong on a first reading, since the reference holds the address of x and x holds 5, but the closing brace ends the life of x, so by the next line the address leads nowhere and printing it would read memory that the program has already given back.

In C that is left to the programmer's care, and in languages with a garbage collector the value is simply kept alive for as long as anything refers to it. Rust works it out before the program runs, by comparing how long each reference is used with how long its value lives, and it refuses any program in which the first outlasts the second. Most of the time it makes the comparison without help, and the notation that sometimes appears in function signatures is how you tell it what a function does with its references.

intro.whyItMatters: Lifetimes are the one place where Rust asks you to say something the compiler cannot work out for itself.

recap.keyIdea: A lifetime is the span in which a reference is valid, and an annotation such as 'a states how the lifetimes of inputs and result relate, so the compiler can check every call.

blocks.text: A reference must not outlive its value, and rustc compares the two with **lifetimes**: E0597 means a value was dropped too early, E0515 means a function returned a reference to its own local variable, and E0106 means that a signature with two input references needs an annotation. The annotation `'a` describes a relation and does not make anything live longer.
Elision rules fill in the annotation for one input reference or for `&self`, and a struct that holds a reference carries a lifetime parameter and cannot outlive its source.

lessons.title: Closures and iterators

lead.text: A short calculation often does not deserve a name and a place of its own. A **closure** is a function written on the spot: the parameters go between vertical bars and the body follows, so `|a, b| a + b` adds two numbers. It can be given a name with `let`, as `add` is in the figure, and called like a function, as `add(2, 3)`. The parameter and return types are normally worked out by the compiler from the way the closure is used, so they need not be written.

A closure can also use the variables around it, which a function cannot. The closure `shift` uses `offset`, a variable made with `let` before it, and it has *captured* that variable. Each call to `shift(5)` reads `offset`, so the result is 15, and the closure carries the value with it wherever it goes. Closures are the usual way to hand a small piece of behaviour to a method, which is what the rest of the lesson shows.

reveal.text: Changing the 3 to a 2 in the line that creates rate changes both calls, and the closure itself needs no edit.

lead.text: A closure is not generic. The compiler works out its parameter and return types from the first call and keeps them, which is why the types could be left out. In the figure, `echo` is first called with 5, so its parameter becomes an integer. The second call passes the text `"five"`, which is not an integer, and rustc reports **error[E0308]**: mismatched types, with the first call marked as the one that settled the type.

If a function must work for several types, write a generic function with a trait bound, as in the lesson before last. A closure is for a particular job in a particular place, and it may use whatever types that job needs, which is why it is the tool for the short arguments to methods.

lead.text: Many programs take one collection and produce another by changing each item. An **iterator** is anything that can hand out its items one at a time: a range such as `1..=5` is one, and so is `v.iter()`, which walks over a `Vec` by reference. The method **map** takes a closure and produces a new iterator whose items are what the closure returns for each original item, and **collect** gathers the items of an iterator into a collection.

In the figure, `v.iter()` yields references to 1, 2 and 3, the closure `|x| x + 1` adds 1 to each, and `collect` puts the results into a `Vec<i32>`. The type of the result has to be stated, here with the annotation on `w`, because `collect` can build many kinds of collection and cannot tell which one is wanted. A method such as `map` is called an **adaptor**, because it returns another iterator, and one such as `collect` or `sum` a **consumer**, because it uses the iterator up.

The method **filter** takes a closure that gives `true` or `false` for each item, and passes on only the items for which it is true. Chained with `map` and ended with the consumer **sum**, it reads like a pipeline: `filter(|n| n % 2 == 0).map(|n| n * 10).sum()`. The figure sends the items 1 to 5 down such a belt. Only 2 and 4 pass the filter, the map turns them into 20 and 40, and `sum` adds them to 60.

Use the second view to take the consumer off the end. Without sum, collect or count, nothing asks for any item, and none of the stages runs. Whatever the chain is, the items go through one at a time, and nothing is built in between: there is no list of the even numbers and no list of the multiples, only one item at a time travelling down the belt.

lead.text: Writing `v.iter().map(...)` does not process anything. It builds a description of the work, and the closure runs only when a consumer pulls items through. The figure's program makes that visible by printing inside the closure. The word `before` comes out first, although the map was written above it, because the map has not run yet. The call to `sum` then pulls the three items through, and the lines `map 1`, `map 2` and `map 3` appear in turn, followed by the total 12.

A chain that ends without a consumer therefore does nothing, and rustc warns about it, with the message that iterators are lazy and do nothing unless consumed. The laziness is an advantage, since a chain over a very long sequence does no more work than the consumer asks for.

reveal.text: rustc warns that the iterator is unused and does nothing unless consumed. The closure's `println!` never ran.
No Vec of long words was ever built: each word went through the filter and was counted as it arrived.

lead.text: The return type tells collect what to build, so the call needs no annotation.

reveal.text: A for loop with push would give the same result, but the chain says what is being done to each item in a single line.

lead.text: A closure borrows the variables it uses by default, which is enough while the variables are still alive. A function that returns a closure has a problem: `n` belongs to `make_adder`, and `make_adder` is over by the time the closure is called. The keyword **move** in front of the closure makes it take its captured variables with it, so the closure owns its own `n` and nothing is left behind. The return type `impl Fn(i32) -> i32` says that the function returns *something that can be called* with an `i32` and gives back an `i32`.

In the figure, `make_adder(5)` returns a closure that adds 5 and `make_adder(0)` one that adds 0, each with its own captured `n`. Calling them with 10 gives 15 and 10. The same idea, a function that builds other functions, is useful whenever a small variation of a calculation has to be passed around as a value.

reveal.text: Without move, rustc refuses the function with E0373: the closure may outlive the variable it borrows.

lessons.orientation: Write closures that capture variables, and chain iterator methods such as map, filter, sum and collect.

blocks.text: Take the numbers from 1 to 6, keep the odd ones, square each and add the squares. In Rust the whole job is one expression, `(1..=6).filter(|n| n % 2 == 1).map(|n| n * n).sum()`, that reads from left to right like the sentence that describes it, with no loop variable, no total to start at zero and no list of intermediate results.

Each stage is a short function written on the spot, called a **closure**, and the stages are joined by a dot. The style rests on two ideas that Rust treats carefully, namely that a closure can use variables from the place where it is written, and that a sequence hands out its items one at a time and does no work until something asks for them.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to write closures that capture variables, and chain map, filter, sum and collect to turn one collection into another.
intro.whyItMatters: Iterator chains replace most hand-written loops with a line that says what is being done.

recap.keyIdea: A closure is a small unnamed function that can capture variables, and iterator adaptors such as map and filter are lazy, so nothing runs until a consumer such as sum, count or collect asks for items.

blocks.text: A **closure** `|x| x + offset` can use the variables around it, and its parameter types are fixed by its first use. Iterators hand out items one at a time, **adaptors** such as `map` and `filter` describe a change, and a **consumer** such as `sum`, `count` or `collect` makes it happen, one item at a time through the whole chain.
A function that returns a closure uses the move keyword and an impl Fn return type, so that the closure owns what it captured.

lessons.title: Putting it together: a score report

lead.text: The task is a small report. A text holds lines of the form name,score, where some lines are good and some are not: one may lack its comma, and another may have a score that is not a number. The program has to read every line, group the good scores by name, report each name's average in alphabetical order, and say which lines it skipped and why. Nothing here is new in itself. What is new is that every part of the course is needed together, and that the shape of the program follows from the types.

The figure shows the path of one line, and the buttons choose a good one and a bad one. The text is split into lines, and each line goes to **parse_line**, which returns a `Result`. A good line becomes an entry and is stored in a map from each name to its list of scores. A bad line is an `Err` carrying a message, which goes to a printed report of what was skipped. Only the map feeds the later stages: the names are sorted, each name's list is averaged, and the averages are printed.

afterFigure.text: The decision about a bad line is made in one place, the match in main, and the functions beneath it only say what happened. That is the design principle of the lesson: let a Result carry bad input up to the code that knows what to do about it.

lead.text: The function takes a `&str` and returns `Result<Entry, String>`, so the type says that it can fail and what the failure looks like. Its first step, **split_once(',')**, cuts the line at the first comma and returns an `Option` of the two halves, and **ok_or("missing comma")** turns that `Option` into a `Result` by supplying the error to use for `None`. The `?` after it returns the `Err` from `parse_line` at once if the comma is missing, so the line `"dee"` ends there with the message `missing comma`.

The second step trims the score and parses it as a `u32`, and **map_err** changes the error that `parse` produces into a `String`, which is the error type this function returns, using `format!` to include the name. The `?` again leaves early on failure. If both steps pass, the last line builds the `Entry` with the trimmed name. The program in the figure feeds three lines through it: a good one, one with a bad score, and one with no comma.

reveal.text: `is_ok()` is true for the `Ok` variant, and `filter` keeps the lines for which it is true, so the count is the number of good lines.
The error message for the bad score is the standard library's own text, passed through `to_string`, so nothing had to be written for it.

lead.text: Grouping scores by name needs a map whose values are lists, a `HashMap<String, Vec<u32>>`. The `entry` method from the lesson on collections finds a name or makes room for it, and **or_default()** fills the room with the default value of the type, here an empty `Vec`, so that `.push(score)` can follow straight away. The one expression `by_name.entry(name).or_default().push(score)` adds a score to a name's list whether or not the name has been seen before.

The figure collects three pairs and prints each name's list. Because the map's order is unspecified, the keys are collected into a `Vec` and sorted before the loop, so that ann comes before bo whatever the map holds. The keys are references to Strings, and indexing the map with `by_name[name]` reads the list for each.

reveal.text: `or_insert(0)` and `+=` gave each name a running total, and a list was never needed.

lead.text: As a program grows, related functions belong together, and Rust groups them in a **module**: `mod stats { ... }` gives a name to the items inside it. Items in a module are private to it unless marked **pub**, so `mean` is written `pub fn` and code outside the module can call it as `stats::mean`. The double colon is the same one that you used for `Coin::Dime` and `Counter::new`, because a module is a name for items in the same way as a type is.

The function `mean` returns an `Option<f64>`, since an empty list has no average and `None` says so, where a division by zero would have produced a meaningless number. It converts the sum and the count to `f64` before dividing, and the format `{m:.1}` in the figure prints the result with one digit after the decimal point, so 9.0 appears for the list 8, 9, 10.

reveal.text: Dividing the two `u32` values directly would have given the whole number 3, and the format `{m:.2}` would then not have applied.
Without pub, rustc would refuse the call with E0603: the function is private.

lead.text: The complete program is in the figure. Read it from the top and it is a tour of the course. The `use` line brings in `HashMap`, and the module `stats` holds `mean`, an `Option` because an empty list has no average. The struct `Entry` models a parsed line, and `parse_line` returns a `Result`, chaining `split_once`, `ok_or`, `parse` and `map_err` with `?`. In `main`, the loop over `data.lines()` borrows each line as a `&str` slice, and the `match` sends a good entry to the map with `or_default().push` and a bad one to a printed message.

After the loop, the keys are collected and sorted so that the report is the same on every run, and for each name the `if let Some(avg)` takes the `Option` apart, so that a name with no scores would print nothing. The output begins with the two skipped lines, in the order in which the lines were read, and then gives ann's average of 8 and 10, which is 9.0, and bo's of 6 and 7, which is 6.5.

afterFigure.text: No rule was bent to make this work. The borrow checker sees names, entries and scores each moved or borrowed in a way that it can verify, and the types make the failures visible: Result for bad input and Option for a missing average.

blocks.text: Data that comes from outside a program is rarely clean. A line such as ann,8 is easy to read, but the next may lack its comma or hold a score that is not a number, and a program that reads many lines has to decide for each one whether to use it or to report it and move on. Here is such a program, about fifty lines long: it groups the good scores by name, prints each person's average in alphabetical order, and says which lines it skipped and why.

At this size the separate rules from the course stop being exercises and start to fit together, because every part of the program rests on one that has already been met. The compiler's checks, which can seem like obstacles in a three-line program, are the reason that a fifty-line one can be changed and still be trusted.

flashcards.front: In Rust, what must you write to give an existing variable a new value with `=`?
flashcards.back: Create it with `let mut`, for example `let mut count = 0;`

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: let mut

flashcards.front: What is it called when a second let reuses a variable's name?
flashcards.back: Shadowing. The new variable hides the old one and may have a different type.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Shadowing

flashcards.front: In Rust, what does 9 / 2 evaluate to?
flashcards.back: 4. Dividing two integers drops the remainder.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 / 2 is 4 with remainder 1, which is dropped.

flashcards.front: A Rust function's last line is `x + 1;` with a semicolon. Why does the function not return `x + 1`?
flashcards.back: The semicolon makes it a statement. Only a final expression without a semicolon is returned.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The semicolon turns it into a statement.

flashcards.front: Which error code does rustc report when the blocks of an if give different types?
flashcards.back: E0308 reports mismatched types, so both blocks of an if must give the same type.

flashcards.front: What happens to the other blocks of an else-if chain once one condition is true?
flashcards.back: They are skipped, because Rust runs only the first block whose condition is true.

flashcards.front: Which range visits 1, 2, 3 and 4: `1..4` or `1..=4`?
flashcards.back: `1..=4`, because the equals sign includes the end value, while `1..4` stops at 3.

flashcards.front: How do you hand a value out of a loop?
flashcards.back: Write `break` followed by the value, as in `break n;`, and `let found = loop { ... }` receives it.

flashcards.front: Which error code reports the use of a value after it was moved?
flashcards.back: E0382: the new owner holds the value, so the old name cannot be used.

flashcards.front: How many owners can a value have at once?
flashcards.back: One. When the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One. When the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped.

flashcards.front: Which error code does rustc report for two mutable borrows of one value that are in use together?
flashcards.back: E0499. A mutable reference must be the only reference to its value.

flashcards.front: Until when does a borrow last?
flashcards.back: Until the last use of the reference, so reordering lines can end a conflict.

flashcards.front: Which parameter type should a function take when it only reads some text?
flashcards.back: `&str`, since it accepts both a literal and a borrowed `String`.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: &str

flashcards.front: Why does Rust refuse `s[0]` on a string?
flashcards.back: Text is UTF-8 and a character may take several bytes, so a byte position is not a character position.

flashcards.front: Which keyword starts the block that holds a struct's methods?
flashcards.back: `impl`, as in `impl Rect { ... }`.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: impl

flashcards.front: Which self kinds does a method use to read, to change and to consume a value?
flashcards.back: `&self` reads, `&mut self` changes, and `self` takes ownership and consumes the value.

flashcards.front: Which error code does rustc report for a match that leaves a variant uncovered?
flashcards.back: E0004: every variant must be covered, or the rest caught by an arm written _.

flashcards.front: Why can a _ arm hide a mistake?
flashcards.back: It keeps the match compiling when a new variant is added, so the compiler stops pointing at the places that need to handle it.

flashcards.front: What are the two variants of `Option<T>`?
flashcards.back: `Some(value)` holds a value of type `T`, and `None` holds no value.

flashcards.front: Which method gives the value inside a Some, or a default when the Option is None?
flashcards.back: `unwrap_or(default)`.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: unwrap_or

flashcards.front: What do the two variants of `Result<T, E>` hold?
flashcards.back: Ok holds the success value of type T, and Err holds the error of type E.

flashcards.front: Which operator returns an Err from the current function, or gives the value inside an Ok?
flashcards.back: The ? operator.

flashcards.front: Which method returns an `Option`, where indexing with `[]` would panic for a missing position?
flashcards.back: `get`: `v.get(i)` is `Some(item)` or `None`.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: get

flashcards.front: How do you add 1 to the count for a word in a `HashMap`, starting it at 0 if it is new?
flashcards.back: `*counts.entry(word).or_insert(0) += 1;`

flashcards.front: Which bound allows a generic function to compare two values of type `T` with `>` and `<`?
flashcards.back: `T: PartialOrd`, the trait that provides the ordering operators.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: PartialOrd

flashcards.front: Why does `fn bigger<T>(a: T, b: T)` fail to compile when it compares `a > b`?
flashcards.back: Inside the body nothing is known about T, so the comparison needs a bound that promises it.

flashcards.front: Which error code reports a reference used after the value it points to was dropped?
flashcards.back: E0597: the value does not live long enough.

flashcards.front: What does a lifetime annotation such as 'a change about how long values live?
flashcards.back: Nothing. It describes how references relate, and the compiler checks that description at each call.

flashcards.front: Which keyword makes a closure take ownership of the variables it uses?
flashcards.back: `move`, as in `move |x| x + n`.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: move

flashcards.front: Why does `v.iter().map(|x| x * 2)` do nothing on its own?
flashcards.back: Adaptors are lazy: the closure runs only when a consumer such as sum, count or collect asks for items.

flashcards.front: Which keyword makes a function inside a module visible from outside it?
flashcards.back: pub, so that code outside can call module::function.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: pub

flashcards.front: Why does the report program have `parse_line` return a `Result` instead of stopping at a bad line?
flashcards.back: A Result carries the bad input up to main, which can report it and carry on with the good lines.
